newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: German gas oil users keep to low stocks policy.
newsitem.headline: German gas oil users keep to low stocks policy.

text.p: The recent low-stocks policy of German gas oil consumers points to a new trend rather than an imminent buying rush, German traders said on Friday.
"We're probably going to see people just stocking up to, say, 50 percent (of capacity)," one German gas oil trader said.

German household stocks of heating oil fell by 2.5 percentage points in November to 62.4 percent of full capacity, compared with 67.7 percent last year and a 15-year historical average of 66.0 percent, according to traders who have seen a confidential monthly report produced for the German oil industry.
The falls were fairly uniform throughout western Germany, they said.
"We've seen the stocks regularly below year-ago levels for a year now," one trader said.

The initial drawdown of stocks was seen last December when a sharp price rise discouraged buying. The harsh winter led to concerted home-heating, while high prices and very high premiums continued to deter buyers.
In the past, traders regarded the monthly stocks figures as an indication of latent demand. The regular habits of consumers meant that any monthly shortfall would lead to fairly rapid restocking.
Now, an increasing number of traders believe the pattern is breaking as consumers become ever more price-sensitive and ever more reluctant to hold large non-performing gas oil stocks.
"(German) people really do not have as much money as they used to have and the gas oil tank is not the priority," said one trader.

Throughout the year, the shortfall has persisted as high product prices have prevailed. Local newspapers have compounded the sales drought by consistently advising against purchases. Only in July and August did buying pick up.
Despite a recent slide, benchmark IPE gas oil futures were around $209.00 a tonne on Thursday, still 25 percent higher than last December.

The dollar/mark exchange rate has also disadvantaged German consumers. A year ago, one dollar was worth 1.45 marks. Today, although the dollar is off early December highs, consumers need 1.54 marks for their dollar's worth of product.
The result is that the German consumer, in Frankfurt for example, is paying around 36 marks per 100 litres of heating oil, compared with 28 marks at the same time last year.

An additional theory to account for the low-stocks policy is that lower domestic freight rates have reduced the fixed cost of deliveries. Consumers will therefore more readily stock up two to three times per year, rather than the traditional annual refill.

"We used to have a standard, uniform cost structure (for road haulage), but rising competition, especially since 1995,.. has seen the freight rates go down. The disadvantage of restocking more than once per one or two years has gone," said one inland trader.
Traders say November and December sales have been well below average for the time of year.
"We have sold about half of the planned quantities in the past month," one said.
However, the real test will come this winter, particularly if cold weather grips the continent.
"They won't look at the prices so much then. They will look at the tanks and the temperatures and they won't want to freeze," one German trader said.
Some traders, however, are not so convinced that the Germans will buy en masse, believing instead that the German consumers will happily see the oil level in their tanks sink.
The question for them is not whether the stocks draw-down will continue, but at what level stocks will stabilise.
-- Philip Blenkinsop, Amsterdam Newsroom, +31 20 504 5004
